paper.title_en: Physics in Safety and Safety in Physics: Lessons from the LHC and its Underground Experiments
paper.abstract_en: Large underground particle-physics facilities are usually discussed by separating scientific performance from the systems that make their operation safe. We develop a complementary view in which safety is treated as an intrinsic part of the physical and operational structure of an experiment. Using the LHC, ATLAS, and CMS as principal case studies, we introduce the concepts of physics in safety and safety in physics: physical laws, measurements, and models determine hazards and protective barriers, while those barriers in turn define the machine, detector, access, and intervention states in which physics can be performed. We formulate this relation through a \emph{safe operational phase space} and through admissible trajectories connecting different configurations, emphasizing that safety constrains not only states but also transitions between them. The framework is applied to beam and magnet protection, cryogenic and oxygen-deficiency hazards, detector-specific risk configurations, personnel access, maintenance, and radiation protection, with particular attention to the different architectures of ATLAS and CMS. We argue that validated protection does not merely restrict scientific activity but can enlarge the domain of sustainable operation. This viewpoint provides a unified physical and operational framework for understanding safety at the LHC and for incorporating protection, maintainability, and recoverability into the design of future accelerator and underground facilities such as HL-LHC, FCC and muon collider.
